0. Executive answer to the training question

Yes. The OCR model can be trained/fine-tuned, and for this project that is one of the highest-value improvements you can make. The recommended path is not to train a giant VLM from scratch. Instead, start from PP-OCRv6 pretrained weights and fine-tune the text-detection and text-recognition components on your own medicine-strip images. PaddleOCR explicitly documents vertical-scene fine-tuning for detection and recognition and recommends starting from pretrained weights. Its documentation says a small amount of real vertical-scene data can materially improve accuracy; it gives >=500 detection samples and >=5,000 recognition samples as practical starting points. [1]

The most important distinction is that detection and recognition are different learning problems. Detection learns where the tiny text is. Recognition learns what the text says. For medicine blister packs, you should train them separately, then measure end-to-end medicine-identification accuracy.
Fine-tune PP-OCRv6 medium detector on annotated blister/strip text boxes/polygons
Fine-tune PP-OCRv6 medium recognizer on cropped blister text lines
Train later only if rules/database matching are insufficient
Use as fallback/semantic verifier first; consider later domain fine-tuning
Do not “train” first; use deterministic decoding (e.g. ZXing-C++)

For the first production version, the architecture recommended by this document is PP-OCRv6 Medium as the primary OCR engine, PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 as a difficult-case fallback, ZXing-C++ for barcodes, OpenCV for image quality and geometry, and a medicine catalog for candidate validation. PP-OCRv6 is the current PaddleOCR universal OCR generation with tiny/small/medium tiers; the medium model is 34.5M parameters and the official documentation highlights improvements for industrial/specialized text. [2][3] PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 is a separate 0.9B document/image VLM released under Apache-2.0 and reports 96.33% on OmniDocBench v1.6, but that benchmark is a document benchmark, not a blister-pack benchmark. [4]

Given a mobile-phone photograph of a medicine blister strip, tablet strip, foil pack, or similar medicine packaging, identify the medicine reliably enough for the application to present a candidate medicine name, strength, manufacturer and supporting evidence, while refusing to guess when confidence is too low.
Recover visible medicine name and strength from very small text.
Recover batch/lot and expiry when readable, but treat them as secondary fields.
Handle perspective distortion, mild curvature, blur, glare, low contrast and foil reflections.
Support multilingual text that the selected OCR model can recognize; specifically test English plus the languages actually present in your target market.
Use multiple pieces of evidence instead of trusting a single OCR string.
Provide deterministic diagnostics explaining why an image was rejected or why the identification is low confidence.
Do not treat OCR as a medical prescribing or dosing engine.
Do not infer a medicine solely from an uncertain fuzzy string match.
Do not claim that a generic OCR benchmark proves performance on blister foil; build and publish an in-domain evaluation set.
Do not make the first version dependent on a 35B document parser when a specialized OCR stack can handle the bulk of requests.
2. Why blister/strip OCR is a special problem

A medicine blister is not a normal document page. The text can be tiny, repeated, curved, partially occluded by pill cavities, printed on reflective foil, stamped or embossed, photographed at a severe angle, or captured at insufficient resolution. The useful text may occupy only a small fraction of the image. The camera can also introduce motion blur, focus blur, lens distortion, white-balance shifts, compression artifacts and specular highlights.

The core design principle is “specialized fast path + semantic fallback + deterministic evidence”. The first OCR model should be cheap enough to run on every request. The 0.9B VLM should only be invoked when the fast path is uncertain or structurally inconsistent.

PP-OCRv6 is the latest generation in PaddleOCR as of this specification. The official documentation describes tiny, small and medium tiers from 1.5M to 34.5M parameters. The medium/small models support a unified 50-language model, and the project highlights improvements in specialized text scenarios such as industrial characters. The official PP-OCRv6 medium recognition configuration uses a PPLCNetV4 backbone with SVTR-LCNet-style recognition components. [2][5]
Small enough for practical server inference compared with a giant VLM.
Better fit than a generic VLM for raw text detection/recognition.
Allows domain-specific training for blister images.
Useful if target medicines contain multiple Latin-script languages.
Enables direct fine-tuning instead of rebuilding the pipeline.
Permissive for common commercial/open-source use; verify all third-party model/data licenses before shipping. [6]
Do not choose the model purely from vendor benchmark claims. Your selection criterion should ultimately be medicine-level identification accuracy on your own held-out blister dataset.

PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 is an Apache-2.0 0.9B image-to-text/document parsing model. The official model card reports a 96.33% OmniDocBench v1.6 score and provides direct PaddleOCR integration. [4] It is useful here as a difficult-case verifier because it can reason over the image rather than only performing line-level OCR, but the project should not assume that a document benchmark translates directly into blister-pack accuracy.

Recommended use: send only a focused blister/foil crop or the best processed image, ask for structured fields, forbid guessing, and compare its result with PP-OCRv6 rather than replacing the specialized OCR engine.
Benchmark as fallback candidate; not first choice without in-domain tests
Benchmark for difficult images if available in your deployment constraints
Do not make it the core OCR path; retain as research/verification option only if it proves useful
Keep as a baseline; not the primary engine

The camera UI should actively help the user produce OCR-friendly images. A scanning rectangle should occupy a useful portion of the preview, and the app should display short instructions such as “Move closer”, “Reduce reflection”, “Hold steady”, or “Place strip inside frame”.
Before inference, compute a quality vector. The exact thresholds must be tuned on your own camera dataset.

Instead of trusting one photo, capture a short burst of 3-5 frames. Rank frames by blur, glare, text/strip coverage and exposure. Run the OCR stack on the top 1-2 frames or use the best frame for the initial pass. This can produce a larger real-world gain than swapping between similarly strong OCR models.
Decode the original image without unnecessary recompression.
Correct orientation using the camera metadata and optional orientation classification.
Downscale only if the source is excessively large; preserve enough pixels for tiny text.
Normalize color space and keep an untouched original for audit/reprocessing.

Detect the medicine strip/blister or a relevant packaging region. The first implementation may use a simple object detector or user-guided crop. A later version can train a lightweight “medicine-pack ROI detector” using the same captured dataset.

If four corners or a stable quadrilateral can be estimated, use a homography to rectify the image. For curved foil, use an optional nonlinear dewarping stage. Do not force dewarping on already-flat images when it introduces distortions.
Preserve model-native evidence and color clues.
Improve local contrast when illumination is uneven.
Recover edges when the source is mildly soft.
Give tiny characters more pixel support; do not invent information.
Do not threshold everything into pure black/white. Foil and embossed text frequently contain useful grayscale gradients that binarization can destroy.

The detector should find text regions, ideally as polygons when text is rotated or slightly curved. Detection is where domain fine-tuning often produces a major gain because generic detectors can miss very small or low-contrast foil text.

The recognizer receives a normalized text-line crop and predicts the transcription. Medicine text tends to contain short words, digits, decimals, units, punctuation and abbreviations, so the character distribution differs from general web/document corpora.

Barcode scanning should run in parallel with OCR, not after OCR failure. Pharmaceutical packaging can use GS1 DataMatrix and other identifiers. GS1 describes the healthcare use of DataMatrix and notes that GS1 identifiers can carry product identifiers such as GTIN plus attributes such as batch/lot, expiry and serial number. [7]
Use ZXing-C++ as the initial open-source reader. The project supports UPC/EAN, Code 128, Data Matrix ECC200 and other retail/industrial/matrix symbologies and provides C++ plus multiple bindings. [8]
-> use barcode evidence in final score
A barcode match can be stronger than OCR text. However, do not assume every barcode payload is a medicine database key without understanding the symbology and country/manufacturer data structure.

The search layer should combine exact matching, normalized matching and conservative fuzzy matching. RapidFuzz or a database trigram index can be used for candidate generation, but candidate acceptance must be evidence-based.
OCR often confuses visually similar characters. Common examples include O/0, I/l/1, S/5, B/8 and punctuation around strengths. Normalization should be context-aware.
Normalize common unit spellings (mg, g, mcg, mL, %, IU) without changing numeric values.
Do not globally replace “I” with “l” or “0” with “O”; use contextual candidate matching.
Keep the original OCR string for auditability.
The application needs a dedicated confidence layer. Model confidence alone is insufficient because a high-confidence OCR string can still correspond to the wrong drug.

The exact formula is not sacred. Train/calibrate it using a held-out dataset. If the application ever displays a medicine recommendation, the product layer should expose why the candidate was selected: e.g. “name matched 98%, strength matched 100%, barcode matched exact”.

If PP-OCRv6 and PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 agree on medicine name and strength, increase confidence. If they disagree, do not average the strings; treat the discrepancy as a review signal and run database candidate ranking.
13. Can we train the OCR model? Yes - detailed training plan

The recommended path is fine-tuning, not training from zero. PaddleOCR provides separate training/evaluation/inference modules and separate configurations for detection and recognition. The PP-OCRv6 medium recognition config currently exposes pretrained weights, a 100-epoch baseline schedule, SVTR_LCNet-based recognition with a PPLCNetV4 medium backbone, multi-scale training and augmentations; the detector has its own configuration. [5][9]
Text region detector specialized for blister foil
Classifies brand/strength/batch/expiry if rule parsing becomes insufficient

PaddleOCR documentation recommends at least 500 real detection samples and at least 5,000 recognition samples as practical starting points for vertical-scene fine-tuning. Treat those as a floor, not a promise of production accuracy. [10]

The best number depends more on diversity than raw count. Ten thousand nearly identical images of one brand are less useful than a smaller dataset spanning many brands, foil colors, fonts, camera devices, angles and lighting conditions.

Keep field labels in your annotation layer even though the OCR detector does not necessarily train on them. They become extremely valuable for analytics, targeted evaluation and future multi-task models.

Create one line crop per text line and an exact transcription. Keep the raw crop, corrected/rectified crop, label, source image id and field type. Field type lets you evaluate medicine names separately from batch numbers.

Do not randomly split near-duplicate images into train and validation sets. If the same medicine strip was photographed 50 times, all 50 variants should stay in one split. A better rule is to split by product/packaging family and by physical capture session/device where possible.
Final report only; never tune on it
Synthetic data is extremely useful for increasing character diversity and stress-testing the exact phenomena that make blister OCR hard. It should augment, not replace, real images.
Render medicine names, strengths, units, manufacturers and batch-like strings using fonts approximating the target packaging.

Apply perspective transforms, local warps and mild curvature.

Add foil-like background textures and specular highlights.
Vary brightness, white balance and color temperature.
Add partial occlusion and pill-cavity shadows.
Generate hard negatives such as logos, symbols, decorative lines and foil texture that should not be recognized as text.
Take product layouts or generic packaging templates and composite the rendered text/foil into realistic scenes. Preserve the exact ground-truth text so the resulting data is automatically labeled.

Start by fine-tuning recognition before touching detection if your detector is already finding the line crops. This is the fastest way to answer “does pharmacy-specific data fix the main character errors?”

The fastest way to start is to implement the inference pipeline with pretrained models before collecting a huge dataset. This tells you which stage is actually failing.
Create a 100-300 image pilot set of real blister/strip photos.
Run PP-OCRv6 Medium on original, contrast, sharpened and rectified variants.

Only then decide where fine-tuning will produce the biggest return.
M4: 2k-5k full photos + 10k-50k crops -> strong v1

These are project-planning milestones, not fixed schedules. The important sequence is baseline -> measure -> annotate -> fine-tune -> measure again.
Do not run a giant VLM on every image and call that the OCR system.
Do not assume document benchmark scores transfer to blister foil.
Do not crop away context before you have stored the original image and coordinates.

Do not evaluate only average OCR accuracy; evaluate medicine-level false identifications.
Do not retrain from scratch unless you have a research reason and substantial data/compute.
34. Direct answer: can we train the OCR model?

Yes - and the project should plan for it from the beginning. The most practical route is to fine-tune PP-OCRv6 Medium’s detector and recognizer on your own annotated blister/strip data. PaddleOCR provides explicit detection and recognition training configurations, and its vertical-scene fine-tuning documentation is specifically intended for cases where a generic pretrained model is not enough. [5][10]

Start with the pretrained model. Do not immediately change the architecture. First establish a baseline on your own test set. Then fine-tune recognition with real text-line crops. After that, fine-tune detection with full-image text polygons. Add realistic foil/glare/perspective synthetic augmentation. Keep a clean held-out test set and compare every new model against the baseline.

If your dataset eventually becomes large enough, you can go beyond simple fine-tuning: train a medicine-specific text detector, a specialized recognizer, or a lightweight candidate-ranking model. But those should be second-stage improvements, not the starting point.

40. Appendix C - example decision for the provided sample

For the representative image used in this specification, the system should not simply OCR the entire 481x341 photograph. It should first isolate the blister/box regions, look for barcodes, and send the blister crop through several image variants. The large printed “Risperdal 2 mg” area is likely easier than the repeated tiny foil text; this example should therefore be included in the benchmark as an easy-vs-hard-region pair.
